points.text_snippet: Tweet: thinking about the long tweet meta. first, it’s a waste to write a tweet that’s only *slightly* long. people have to click an extra time to read the rest of a long tweet past the first 280 chars. so the game is to invite people to make the click  so the first 280 chars should be a good advertisement for the rest of the long tweet; it should promise the reader that something interesting is waiting, and then the rest of the long tweet should deliver on that promise. so no 300 character tweets unless somehow the last 20 characters are an amazing punchline; that’s not worth the extra click to your readers  second, a question any long tweet has to answer is: why isn’t this a thread? i personally have really enjoyed learning how to write threads well, it’s a distinct form of writing with its own distinct advantages. the key fact about threads, which i was introduced to by @visakanv’s twitter_rpg_strategy_guide.txt, is that any individual tweet in a thread can be RT’d or QT’d, by anyone, including yourself. (also that any individual tweet can itself be a QT!)  what this means is that it’s worth learning how to write threads in such a way that every individual tweet stands somewhat on its own, and makes sense and says something comprehensible even when RT’d / QT’d outside the context of the rest of the thread. ideally (imo) each tweet in a thread should make exactly one point or introduce exactly one new idea - they get very cluttered if you try to say too much at once. the thread as a whole serves as a journey through the individual ideas or points in each tweet, and can also offer detours via QTs to other threads. one of the cool things learning how to thread like this does is that you can be surprised by which tweets in a thread resonate with other people - maybe you had a grand conclusion but it’s a throwaway tweet in the middle that people actually RT and QT and reply to. this is a level of granularity of feedback on your writing and ideas that longform doesn’t support by default (although google doc comments can be even more granular, eg) and i’ve learned a lot from it  from this perspective long tweets offer a return back to longform, but somewhat more casual longform than eg a ‘stack post. sometimes you wanna describe an idea that takes longer than 280 chars to meaningfully express. sometimes you wanna ramble and think out loud in a less structured way than a thread (this is what i’m doing rn). threads also have the disadvantage that if you do too good a job making the individual tweets stand alone then when they get RT’d and QT’d they may not even look like part of a thread, so people may not even click through to the rest of it. long tweets have the advantage (and disadvantage) that the whole thing is RT’d or QT’d at once, meaning it’s harder to single out individual bits but the whole package gets transported around twitter together, and unlike an external link it’s all still happening on twitter. typically when i write long threads the first tweet gets RT’d and QT’d the most and all the numbers drop off from there. so i’m interested in the ability of long tweets to preserve what might otherwise be a chopped-up thread as more of an organic whole. anyway that’s what i’ve got so far, time to get some food now. thanks for reading  Annotation: The Long Tweet Meta: Qiaochu's analysis of when to thread vs long-tweet, explicitly crediting the guide for teaching him threading mechanics—showing 6 years of compound learning from the original artifact
points.annotation: The Long Tweet Meta: Qiaochu's analysis of when to thread vs long-tweet, explicitly crediting the guide for teaching him threading mechanics—showing 6 years of compound learning from the original artifact

And it has three great advantages. First, it has control of the voice and the means of argument: the three Ls - language, logic and linearity - are all ultimately under left-hemisphere control. It is like being the Berlusconi of the brain: a political heavyweight who has control of the media. Of course we tend to listen more to what it has to say. By understanding these categories, individuals can better navigate their expectations and respond appropriately to unexpected events. points.text_snippet: Tweet: Last year in June, I dropped the default behavior of resisting “negative” emotions. I posted at the top [1], declaring that I no longer suffered. It’s been over a year since then, and that original statement wasn’t 100% accurate. More like 97%.  Since last June, there’s been a handful of emotional and a couple physical experiences that have caused me to suffer. A ten hour tattoo session, McDonalds binge that triggered stomach pain and returning cancer fear, indoor olympics performance issue caused much shame and disappointment, intense waves of prolonged fear caused by airplane turbulence [2], and a few other periods I’m sure happened but I didn’t log. So about ten or less days where I suffered. 355/365 days, or 97% of the rest of the year I didn’t suffer.  I mean suffering with a capital S. What remained after that shift in June didn’t feel like I was Suffering. What remained included occasional slight, subtler meh-ness here and there, slight unsatisfactoriness. Calling those “suffering” feels inaccurate, like it trivializes the level of suck I felt when experiencing the components I bundled up in what I called “negative” emotions in the past. And those subtler ouchies that prevent 100 proof peace have dissolved more and more in the momentum gained from that before-after event last June.  Why have some moments still caused suffering? Maybe there’s experiences that are rare and trigger dusty conditioning which hasn’t been rewritten yet, where the logic behind resistance to emotional experience still lingers. Some patterns of my experience support that idea.  Or perhaps certain levels of combined duration and intensity of “negative” emotions still cause suffering, that the June shift just raised the capacity much higher but not all the way to account for the full range of what god’s gonna gift me. Some patterns of my experience support that idea, but maybe it’s also a characteristic of the former, where high levels of both duration and intensity of “negative” emotion trigger not-updated code.  I didn’t need off-retreat deterministic access to higher jhanas or multiple cessations or 35 noticings per second to stop resisting emotions, just a sporadic practice of looking in direct experience in specific ways (for like four months). But deterministic access to the second jhana, and the emotional work needed to get high without drugs, certainly helped weaken resistance to emotions.  It’s exciting that the jhanas are more widely known, even if still much an open secret outside meditation/tech twitter. And that it’s possible to nix the default assumptions causing emotional resistance using seemingly simple inquiry practices, or most suffering, is an even bigger open secret.  There’s a handful of other folks who publicly share that they've reproduced the results I’m talking about using the same practices, and I hope lots more do so. The shift last June has been the biggest upgrade to my wellbeing, but I’m not a special person who did something exceedingly hard. You can drop emotional resistance too, and there can be lots of ease and enjoyment along the way.  It took me a long time to experience my first jhana, and now most people learn in a week via Jhourney [3]. I hope a similar quickening happens with these inquiry practices.  I don’t know if how I feel is permanent, but over a year is great, and I don’t know why it’d stop being this way anytime soon. I’d love to help others drop default resistance to emotion using jhanas and inquiry. I’m doing more 1:1 calls with folks when I’m not working Jhourney retreats. The accompanying tweet discusses the author's journey of overcoming emotional resistance and achieving a state of deep okayness, sharing their experience and inviting others to do the same.  Annotation: Blissbrah's one-year update: '97% no suffering' with systematic practice documentation, validating the approach

points.text_snippet: Tweet: I always wondered how my NYC community would perform in an emergency situation. We got a test of that last night!  At 8:53pm, @__drewface called me and a few of his closest friends. He said that he'd arrived home to a flooded apartment. His wife was abroad, his baby daughter was freaking out, and he needed help ASAP before mold started growing  Within 10 minutes, we had 7 people on their way to his house. Soon after we had a coordinating WhatsApp group that grew to 14 people @evodevotee was an hour away so she became the Guy In The Chair, using LLMs to come up with a checklist operating procedure for our converging team. She was joined by @madhu___s to figure out purchases of equipment from Home Depot  Meanwhile @MarkEstefanos took off on his electric skateboard to go pick them up  A big group of us show up all at once at the apartment. @IvanVendrov came with smoothies. @beana_tweets came with her boyfriend. I came with Poli, my rockstar friend visiting from Berlin We went downstairs to assess the damage. The bottom floor was now a pond about 1inch deep. Lots of furniture, fabrics, and electronics were sitting in water The source of the flooding was a low-set window. The water had streamed in during the torrential downpour a couple hours previous  We got to work: • We created a human chain to move wet stuff to dry places. • In the absence of a mop, @beana_tweets used a broom to usher water into the floor drain we uncovered. • Poli mopped the floor; she used diluted bleach to clean away runoff water residue, making the floor fit for Andrew's baby to crawl on the next day  In parallel: • @mr_samosaman went knocking on neighbor's doors to borrow a charge-card to operate the laundry machines • @pee_zombie brought a wet/dry vacuum from @fractaltechnyc • I also put on music bc our crew's tacit philosophy is that work can be fun  Finally @MarkEstefanos arrived with the materials to finish the job. These included absorbent towels, gloves, moisture absorbing gel, and four fans that dried the mopped floors extremely fast  As the fans ran, I biked to a place nearby that has the best birria in Brooklyn and picked up tacos, tostadas, and mulitas  We ate them to celebrate (that's @MarkEstefanos holding the bag of birria) In the end, @danielgolliher arrived to help, but we had no more tasks for him. Our crew of 10 had conquered the job in about 2hrs  Some takeaways: 1. Supercoordinaion is possible: I came away impressed by: • how many friends showed up • the speed with which they arrived late on a Wednesday night • how fluidly the group coordinated. No one stood around waiting to be directed – each person was independently sensing for what next things needed to be done. Then they did it, enlisting help if needed  2. LLMs are amazing in emergencies: We used them to quickly create plans, like: "Here's the situation: [context dump]. Come up with an operation procedure for a team of 8 amateurs to handle it." They also answered super specific questions on the fly, like "Should we turn off the HVAC system to prevent mold spores from traveling?"  3. The power of friendship: real  Additional thanks to Ian & Sunil, who wanted to volunteer but we already had too many people. Also to @feral_eyes, who lives all the way in CDMX but who volunteered to cover costs from afar  Btw in case you're reading this, thinking "Wow, there's some crazy magic or luck going on there" – you're wrong!  My friends and I spent a few years figuring out the playbook for how to create a community where people actually show up for one another. I'll post the story of that below because I hope other folks find a way to replicate it. I want a society where ppl have each other's backs  💗  https://t.co/DQxGGp6IJv Images: - [Image #0] The image is a photograph of a person's leg and foot, wearing a red sock, standing on a wooden floor. The room is well-lit, with a couch in the foreground and various items scattered about, including bags and boxes. - [Image #2] The image shows a group of five people in a living room, smiling and holding drinks. The man on the left is taking a selfie, wearing a black shirt with red roses, while the others are seated on a couch behind him, with one holding a yellow bag and another holding a bottle. - [Image #3] The image shows a screenshot of a WhatsApp group chat. points.text_snippet: Tweet: Most women are not (and never will be) capable of telling the truth, because they simply have not grown up enough to stop viewing "the truth" as "what I meant when I said the words."  You say "are you hungry?" And she says "no." You go get food for you and not for her. She is angry. "Why didn't you get me anything?"  "Because you said you weren't hungry."  "But I WAS hungry! I just didn't want to make you feel like you had to get me anything! But I wanted you to!" (So therefore, I did tell the truth.)  This also translates to politics. "I want to live in a diverse country" often means "I don't want to be mean to people by saying I don't." Then they go vote for what they don't want, hoping that they'll get what they do want. Then they don't get it, and it's your fault.  Furthermore, they don't know that you're not doing this.  "I'm not hungry" means "Of course I'm hungry, you should always get me food." You're supposed to know that, because you should imagine being her. Would you be hungry? Yes you would.  So when she says "no," it means "I don't want to be in charge of you getting me food, but you better know I want it and bring some."  Then, when you don't, you OBVIOUSLY knew she wanted food and chose to not get her any. Because you would have been hungry if you were her. So now she's mad.  It is much, much, much easier for men to understand how women communicate than the opposite. For a man to understand a woman, ADD EMOTION. For a woman to understand a man, you have to SUBTRACT EMOTION. This does not compute with women. "Take away all of the feelings from the words and listen to the words."  "But... I still HAVE feelings."  "Right, don't listen to them."  "But I feel like you should know what I feel."  With a large percentage of women, you're not getting anywhere with that. But as a man, you can learn to stop and think: "what would she be feeling when she says this?" Usually, it's as easy as: "what would I be feeling?"  Try it! Next time you're talking with a woman, imagine what she'd be feeling with each message she sends. Then, when you find one that doesn't match what she said, follow the feeling. If you get it right, you might just understand why they vote for all this ridiculous shit.  Annotation: HoeMath's Gender Communication Thread: The signifier/signified distinction applied to male/female miscommunication at scale
points.annotation: HoeMath's Gender Communication Thread: The signifier/signified distinction applied to male/female miscommunication at scale

Instead of spending so much time exploring recursive "deep structures," instead you look for generator functions  You can see generator functions most clearly in people who are having a bad trip on psychedelics or via psychosis: they keep generating new reasons to be paranoid. If it turns out the government isn't watching them, then it's actually that evil spirits toying with them, etc.  Just keep in mind that – if you try to analyze the structure of a generator function – it will often go brrrrr on itself, and generate infinite recursive structure for you explore. Often better to hold off on analysis when you find it, and instead just lovingly "sit" with it / find the presence of awareness within it instead of trying to understand it  (Analysis also sometimes has the negative side effect of calcifying this structures through reification. It's like you turn a changeable ~liquid thing – the generator function – into a stable solid thing. And then you're stuck with a solid thing yikes. Luckily loving presence can convert it back to liquid)  Annotation: First synthesis: Tyler proposes 'generator functions' as the efficient alternative to exploring recursive structures

points.text_snippet: Tweet: As an experiment, I am renouncing the view that I am an amalgam of differently motivated Parts. Instead, I am a unitary Will  As a unitary Will there is no such thing as “being blocked” (eg unable to write or do admin or relax) due to conflicting motivations  Instead there are three options:  Yes: I will do X (bc I want to)  No: I won’t do X (bc I don’t want to)  Simmer/percolate/marinate: I will postpone the decision of whether to do X right now. Maybe I need more information or I’m not in a good state to decide. So I postpone, understanding that I am CHOOSING inaction  Important for this approach: there is *no inner conflict* because there is only one Will (albeit you might be confused about how to channel it bc you are complex). It helps to get in touch with the *experience* of that unitary Will. It will typically be much bigger/wider than your ordinary sense of yourself  Had tried this for a day so far, modeling myself as a unitary Will feels much cleaner than the IFS-style introspection I was doing before. I’m pretty sure that by imagining that I consisted of conflicting Parts that I was hallucinating all sorts of inner conflict the way an LLM would if you prompted it to mediate between parts. (In a mediation frame, conflict is *assumed*)  Try it & report back  or [emblematic of what I truly actually want to be doing]]  Annotation: Practical application: Tyler experiments with renouncing IFS 'Parts' model in favor of unitary Will (Jan 2025)
points.annotation: Practical application: Tyler experiments with renouncing IFS 'Parts' model in favor of unitary Will (Jan 2025)

points.text_snippet: Tweet: There’s an emerging branch of mystical Christianity that is very intriguing. I think of it as “Imaginal Christianity” (IC). You could also call it Mythic Christianity or Jungian Christianity  IC’s main selling point is that it’s compatible with a scientific mindset. I list the tenets I’ve observed below. By doing so, I try to document what I see ppl practicing. (I am not an Imaginal Christian.)  God = the ground of being. It is both presence and void, shows its love by embracing all things that exist & affording the path to salvation through communion with it  “The Lord”: a useful anthropomorphism of god. ICs use imagination to turn something incomprehensible (god) into an imaginal presence that we can speak to and which speaks to us through words, silence, and beyond  Jesus of Nazareth: a person who came much closer than most people to theosis – ie embodying how god would behave if it acted in human form with full recognition of its own nature. By doing so, Jesus genuinely did show us a path to salvation. (Although – here’s the heretical part – other people like Gautama Buddha might show us a complementary paths.) Thanks to the degree that Jesus was charismatic and the degree to which his followers admired him, they created and/or realized an imaginal being called Christ  Christ: a mind that continues to guide humans to salvation, directly inspired by Jesus of Nazareth (whose body is now dead). There are many names for the nature of this type of mind: thoughtform, tulpa, egregore, archetype, living symbol, yidam, memetic entity. His metaphysical status is similar to the way Tibetan lamas seem to regard their deities, as manifestations of Mind. This doesn’t make him less divine; he represents a latent divine potential available to all people. We see archetypes similar to Christ manifest across cultures: Osiris, Dionysus, Krishna, etc. However, Christ is is our culture’s instantiation of the archetype – his specific teachings and the story of his life are meaningful to us  The Bible: to be interpreted symbolically and read as a source of deep wisdom. Its story and teachings contain metaphors that powerfully interact with our collective consciousness. It is not read as an account of 100% literal happenings. It is also understood that the bible is contextual, created for a particular time and place, so it’s up to us to do careful translation and understand how to adapt it to our own context  Miracles & the supernatural: there is agnosticism about the metaphysical status of such things (eg virgin birth, the resurrection, heaven). They are at least seen as helpful metaphors. Some people who practice IC just shrug their shoulders and embrace mystery around the supernatural. Others attempt to retcon it through explanations that are compatible with scientific materialism (eg the idea that Jesus was a master bodyworker able to induce psychosomatic healing; or that hell is real but only as a state of mind)  Christ consciousness/Imitatio Christi: similar to Tibetan yidam practice, you can use imagination to take on the aspect/energy/mind of Christ. (Romans 13:14 – “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ”.) You can also do this with other imaginal beings like Mother Mary, Saint Francis, etc  Prayer: depending on who you ask, prayer is either: (a) prompt engineering for your unconscious (you adopt benevolent intentions and they unconsciously affect behavior in positive and sometimes contagious ways) (b) heart-led concentration meditation similar to metta (c) interfacing with positive imaginal entities like Christ or angels or your personal anthropomorphism of god (d) other things, or all of the above  Overall, I think IC is a positive development. Trad Christians will probably see it as quite heretical. And in my next post, I list some ways it could go wrong. But it could provide shared meaning to millions of Westerners who would otherwise be depressive atheists. IC harnesses the mythic language that people in the West already grew up with  Annotation: Application to 'Imaginal Christianity': Tyler uses framework to analyze emerging mystical Christian movement (Jun 2025)
points.annotation: Application to 'Imaginal Christianity': Tyler uses framework to analyze emerging mystical Christian movement (Jun 2025)

points.text_snippet: Tweet: WAYS I SEE IMAGINAL CHRISTIANITY GOING WRONG:  Going Schizo with Entities Christianity offers a whole cinematic universe of entities: angels, demons, Satan, etc. Similar to Christ, these are seen by ICs as imaginal beings who have their own partial autonomy in our collective consciousness. This is where I see IC practitioners going REAL crazy. They attribute way too much power to these entities, not understanding the degree to which they are belief-mediated. So the more power you believe a mental “demon” has, the more power you give it. I watch people engaging in all sorts of elaborate “magical” practices here to navigate the world of entities. I recommend instead just dissolving their supposed influence through practices of love, prayer, logic, clowning, or Buddhist-style emptiness. These practices are way less ego-pleasing than a narrative that you are engaged in magical trials with powerful entities. But they are less likely to drive you crazy  Procedural Generation of Mental Content Similar to my last point, it’s important to recognize that the mind is really good at making stuff up. You might start practicing IC, and then start believing that “the angels told me to buy crypto” or “Satan made me behave badly toward my mom.” I think a better recipe for sanity is to hold the paradoxical belief there are mental entities who can guide you AND it’s also often just your imagination inventing nonsense. (See quoted post)  Christian Sinning 2.0 IC mostly just changes the metaphysical status of elements of Christianity, making them palatable to the modern mind. IC might still attract and create practitioners who fall victim to the worst Christian sins: self-righteousness & moralizing; judgement of outgroups; self-coercion, repression, and shame; establishment of oppressive hierarchies, and so on. It will take a broader effort to dissolve these negative patterns that seem to have plagued Christianity since it became entangled with state power  Annotation: Synthesis: Tyler warns ICs about 'procedural generation of mental content' while acknowledging utility of imaginal practices
points.annotation: Synthesis: Tyler warns ICs about 'procedural generation of mental content' while acknowledging utility of imaginal practices

points.text_snippet: Tweet: It's not trauma release. it's tension release.  Trauma is a story. Just because there is tension doesn't mean there is or was "trauma." Again, #downwiththetraumanarrative @dberceli  Annotation: Critical Counter-narrative: Leah questioning the 'trauma' framing, arguing it's tension release not trauma release—important conceptual pushback
